_meta: Twenty hypothetical repeated experiments, each estimating the same true value with its own sample mean and 95% confidence interval, used to show that '95% confidence' is a property of the PROCEDURE across many intervals -- about 95% of the intervals it produces contain the true value -- not a probability about any single interval, which either contains the true value or does not. A confidence interval is computed as the sample mean plus or minus z times the standard error. The tempting reading of '95% confidence interval' is 'there is a 95% probability the true value lies in THIS interval,' and it is wrong: the true value is a fixed number and the interval is a fixed range once computed, so the true value is either inside it (probability 1) or outside it (probability 0) -- there is no 95% about it. What the 95% describes is the long-run behavior of the method: if you repeated the experiment many times, about 95% of the intervals it generates would cover the true value and about 5% would miss. On this fixture the true value is 100, each experiment has a standard error of 1.0, and the 95% interval is the mean plus or minus 1.96: of the twenty experiments, nineteen intervals contain 100 (95% coverage) and one, with a sample mean of 102.3, gives the interval 100.34 to 104.26, which does not contain 100 at all -- for that interval, the statement 'there is a 95% chance the truth is inside' is not just imprecise, it is false, since the truth is definitely outside. The true value, the standard error, the z multiplier, and the twenty sample means are the fixture; each interval, whether it contains the truth, and the overall coverage are computed. Stdlib only.
